analysis.one_liner: Lets companies classify gig workers as independent contractors under a tax-code safe harbor.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors and never got a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a test into the tax code under which a worker who meets it must be treated as an independent contractor, not an employee — meaning the company owes no employer payroll taxes and the worker is responsible for all taxes on the pay. Companies that follow the test, sign written contracts, and file the required reports would be largely shielded from IRS efforts to reclassify those workers as employees and collect back taxes. It pairs this with some worker-facing items: 5% tax withholding on the first $20,000 of pay, written contracts spelling out who owes the taxes, and a new right for workers to ask the U.S. Tax Court to decide their status. It never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Gig-economy platforms and any business that hires independent contractors would gain a statutory safe harbor: if they meet the test, they owe no employer-side payroll taxes and the IRS generally could not claw back back-taxes for misclassified workers. Companies would also get lighter paperwork in places — the threshold for reporting payments to the IRS rises from $600 to $1,000, and goods-selling marketplace platforms would only have to report a seller's transactions above $5,000 or 50 per year. Workers who qualify would get written contracts stating they owe their own taxes, 5% withholding on the first $20,000 of pay to help set money aside, and standing to petition the Tax Court over their status. Promotional-products salespeople would be added to the existing "direct seller" category that is excluded from employment-tax treatment.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a test that, once met, legally requires treating a worker as an independent contractor for tax purposes — the company is not an employer, and the pay is not employment compensation — giving businesses certainty against IRS reclassification.

Blocks the IRS from imposing back employment-tax liability on companies that used qualifying written contracts, filed the required reports, and paid over applicable taxes; any reclassification takes effect only going forward, from a 'notice date' 30 days after the IRS first notifies them.

Requires written contracts that tell workers, in writing, that they are responsible for their own federal, state, and local taxes including self-employment taxes, and makes company reporting conditional on actually filing the required information returns.

Requires companies to withhold 5% of a contractor's pay on the first $20,000 per year and send it to the IRS, and lets workers themselves petition the U.S. Tax Court for a determination of their employment status — a right previously available mainly to companies.

Cuts reporting burdens: the threshold for reporting payments to the IRS doubles from $600 to $1,000, and goods-selling marketplace platforms would only report a seller once payments exceed $5,000 or 50 transactions in a year.

analysis.who_pays: Workers classified under the safe harbor would bear the full self-employment tax — both the employee and employer halves of Social Security and Medicare — and, because the pay would not count as employment compensation, would lose tax benefits tied to employee status, such as employer-provided fringe benefits. The withholding backstop covers only the first $20,000 of annual pay, leaving earnings above that untaxed at the source. The Treasury would forgo payroll-tax revenue to the extent companies shift workers into contractor status, and the IRS would lose some of the information reports it uses to verify income, since the reporting thresholds would rise and many small marketplace sellers would drop below them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Contractors and the federal payroll-tax base

drawbacks.text: The safe harbor would push the full employment-tax burden onto workers: they pay both halves of Social Security and Medicare, and because the pay would no longer count as employment compensation they lose employee-status tax benefits. The 5% withholding only applies to the first $20,000 a year, so most gig earnings would still go uncollected at the source.

The reclassification limits would shield companies from retroactive tax bills and penalties even in close cases, as long as they had contracts, filed reports, and showed a 'reasonable basis' for treating workers as contractors — a protection worker-side enforcers would not have.

The bill reduces the information the IRS receives: the 1099 reporting threshold doubles from $600 to $1,000, and goods-selling marketplace platforms would not have to report a seller's activity until payments top $5,000 or 50 transactions, making income from small-scale gig selling easier to go unreported.

Because this is a tax-code safe harbor, its effects would be hard to see: a company could satisfy it with paperwork while the underlying work looks like ordinary employment, and workers who sign the required contract would be agreeing, in writing, to their own non-employee treatment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real but narrow gains: written contracts, a small amount of withholding, and Tax Court access give contractors some clarity and modest protection. But the core of the bill runs the other way — it would make it cheaper and safer for companies to keep workers out of employee status, shifting payroll taxes onto the workers themselves and cutting the IRS's visibility into gig income. The worker-facing provisions are partial offsets to a bill whose main effect is reducing employer tax obligations and audit exposure. As drafted it is lopsided toward the businesses that would use the safe harbor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Thune introduced the bill on March 7, 2019; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No other senator signed on — the cosponsor list stayed at zero — and the Finance Committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the 116th Congress.
The bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the main beneficiaries of the outcome are gig workers, who were spared a law that would have made contractor status easier to lock in and shifted payroll-tax burdens onto them. Gig platforms gained nothing but lost nothing — they continue operating under existing classification rules and audit risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gig workers, who kept existing classification rules

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Dakota; sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, on which he serves; no senator joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up in committee — no hearing, markup, or vote after it was referred; the bill sat for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican introduced the bill, no senator of either party cosponsored it, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee never acted, so there was never a vote to reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have given these platforms a statutory safe harbor making contractor status immune from IRS reclassification and back employment-tax claims — the core financial risk of their business model. The gain comes at workers' expense: contractors pay both halves of Social Security and Medicare and lose employee-status tax benefits.

industries.industry: Businesses using independent contractors in any industry
industries.note: The safe harbor is not limited to app-based work — any company could use qualifying written contracts and reporting to avoid employer payroll taxes and retroactive reclassification, shifting those costs onto workers and the tax base.

The bill defines 'marketplace platform' and raises the reporting threshold for goods-sellers to $5,000 or 50 transactions, cutting their paperwork. The trade-off is that the IRS receives far less information about small sellers' income.

The bill adds salespeople of promotional products to the existing 'direct seller' category excluded from employment-tax treatment, extending a long-standing carve-out to a new set of commission-based sellers.
